notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg103.1st1K-gr: The edition marks lacunae after 'Hippocrates' (ὡσαύτως Ἱπποκράτει φαίνεται γινώσκων . . .) and after 'no longer quite so confidently'; rendered [...]. The bracketed words [οὔτε τούτων τις οὔτε τῶν ἄλλων] are bracketed in the edition, probably as an intrusion. 'Aristotle of Mytilene' is a Peripatetic contemporary of Galen, otherwise little known. νόσον read as νόσου. ἀσυνηθείας is repeated in the Erasistratus quotation (dittography); translated once. In the Hippocrates quotation ὀπός and καυλός are taken as the juice and stalk of silphium. ξυγκομιστοί (loaves) taken as coarse, unbolted bread. ἐπῶν ἰάμβων may mean 'epic verses and iambics'. In the final list the pairs (e.g. ἀλουσίας λουτρῶν) are taken as contrasting alternatives.

In 2.1 the sentence 'all these matters have been discussed at greater length in the examination of the natural faculties' repeats an earlier remark almost verbatim; the text may be doubled here. The phrase 'not only harmless but even useful' refers to plants changed by transplanting; Galen likely has in mind the Persian peach story. In 3.1 'εἱληθερῆ' (sun-heating, basking) is rendered 'sun-heating'.

In 4.1 'μένην, μένην' is a dittography, read once. In 5.1 the bracketed 'ἢ διὰ ῥινός' is marked by the edition as suspect; kept in brackets. 'κακοχυμία' rendered 'bad state of the humours'/'bad humours'.

nodes.text: Although not only the best physicians but all people consider that one of the aims of therapy is also the one taken from habits, some of those who do damage to everything good try to discredit it, asking us why someone who was harmed, as it might happen, on first use by eating beef, and was then compelled to eat it every day for a whole year, would either no longer be harmed at all or be harmed less than those unaccustomed [to it]. Then, overturning by argument whatever we say, they think that with this they have also abolished the existence of the thing itself, just as if someone who had contradicted all the opinions about how we see should refuse to grant that we see at all. Now, that the part taken from habits is of the greatest weight for the discovery of remedies is plainly evident; and for this reason Hippocrates wrote in the Aphorisms: "Those accustomed to bearing their usual labours, even if they are weak or old, bear them more easily than the unaccustomed who are strong and young"; and he went through at greater length in On Regimen in Acute Diseases both the harms from an unaccustomed regimen and the benefits from an accustomed one; and Erasistratus likewise, in the second book On Paralysis, evidently holds the same view as Hippocrates about all habits [...]. And besides, there is none of the ancient physicians who seems to have stated an agreed and incontestable cause [neither of these nor of the others]. For those who seem to have found a plausible one have each found it for one kind of material, some for foods only, some for exercises or occupations, but no one for all kinds of material. Indeed, concerning the giving of cold water too, which we often do in those with acute disease, some oppose us, forbidding it to be given to those with fever and bidding us be content with the indications from the other aims, such as from the affected places and the condition in them, from age, country and season, and further from the mixture and strength of the patient himself, which we are accustomed to use; they say it is ridiculous if, when the liver or lung or stomach or some other of the parts so vital is inflamed, we allow the cold-water drinker to take a cold drink for no other reason than habit (for this, they say, is like allowing those so accustomed to bathe in cold water if they had a fever), as though we allowed all who are sick in whatever way to do everything they are used to, and did not rather take in the aim from habits in addition to all the other aims. Aristotle of Mytilene, for instance, a man who was foremost in Peripatetic philosophy, having fallen into a disease that could have been helped by drinking cold water, because he had never taken such a drink, prevented those who advised him to drink, saying that he knew clearly that he would be seized with convulsions if he tasted cold water; for he said he had seen this happen in another man who had a bodily condition and mixture like his own and the habit of drinking hot water. If he had had the habit of such a drink, as some do, he would most likely not have feared taking it himself; but since he had in fact suffered this, let the physicians present have left him entirely alone. So that man died in this way, as I learned; and when those who had been with him at his death asked me whether, as I had dared with others, giving cold water to some through the whole disease and to others at a certain critical moment while the physicians were wary, I would have dared so in his case too, or whether the man had judged his own nature well, I answered them that he had judged it accurately. For he was very lean and had had a very cold mouth of the stomach from the beginning, so that he would hiccup at once if he was ever chilled even slightly. But just as this man could not have borne a cold drink because of both his habit and the nature of his body, even though the disease indicated it, so I gave it to others quite confidently, even if the one drinking was in an intense burning fever, provided no internal organ was evidently inflamed, though no longer quite so confidently [...]; but after first telling the patient's family that if he did not drink cold water the man would certainly die, but if he drank he would have good hopes of recovery, I gave it in this way, and, God willing, all who took it were saved. So since the remedy has been tested by long experience, we must go on to the search for the cause, having first recalled what Hippocrates wrote in On Regimen in Acute Diseases and Erasistratus in the second book On Paralysis. Hippocrates' passage runs thus: "But it is easy to learn that a poor regimen of food and drink which is always consistent with itself is on the whole safer for health than if one suddenly made a great change to another, better one; since both for those who eat twice a day and for those who eat once, sudden changes bring harm and weakness. Those who have not learned to take a midday meal, if they take one, it at once makes weak and heavy in the whole body, and feeble and sluggish; and if they also take supper after it, [they get] sour belching; and some might even get diarrhoea, when the belly, accustomed to dry out and not to be distended twice nor to cook the food twice, has carried a load contrary to habit." Then, after inserting in between how one might cure the harm from these things, he joins on again about those who have departed from habit and writes thus: "Such a person would suffer still more if he ate three times a day to satiety, and still more if more often; and yet there are many who easily bear eating abundantly three times a day, if they are so accustomed. But also those who have learned to eat twice a day, if they do not take a midday meal, are weak and feeble and timid for any work, and have heartburn. For their innards seem to them to hang, and they pass hot, greenish urine, and the stool is burnt up; in some the mouth also becomes bitter, the eyes become hollow, the temples throb and the extremities grow cold; and most of those who have missed the midday meal cannot eat up their supper; and having supped, they weigh down the belly and sleep badly, much more than if they had taken the midday meal beforehand. Since, then, such things happen to the healthy because of a change of regimen contrary to habit for half a day, it appears profitable neither to add nor to take away. If, then, this man, who contrary to habit ate once, having had empty vessels the whole day, should sup as much as he was accustomed, it is likely that, if he then suffered and was weak from missing the midday meal, and was heavy when he had supped, he would be weighed down much more; and if, having had empty vessels for a longer time, he suddenly took supper afterwards, he would be weighed down still more." After this Hippocrates again, as before, having written of certain corrections of the harm that occurs in those who have had empty vessels contrary to habit, next says again thus: "One might also mention many other things akin to these concerning the belly: how people easily bear the foods they are accustomed to, even if they are not good by nature, and likewise drinks; and bear with difficulty the foods they are not accustomed to, even if they are not bad, and likewise drinks. And as for what much meat-eating, eaten contrary to habit, does, or garlic or silphium or its juice or stalk, or other such things having great powers of their own, one would wonder less if such things cause pains in the belly more than others; but if you were to learn how much trouble and swelling and griping and wind barley cake causes the belly when eaten contrary to habit by one accustomed to eat bread, or what heaviness and distension of the belly bread [causes] in one accustomed to eat barley cake, or what thirst bread itself, eaten hot, causes, and sudden fullness, because it is drying and slow to pass; and what different effects from one another very pure and unbolted [loaves] produce when eaten contrary to habit; and barley cake that is dry contrary to habit, or moist or sticky; and what effect fresh barley meal has on those not accustomed to it, and the other kind on those accustomed to the fresh; and wine-drinking and water-drinking suddenly changed into each other contrary to habit, and watery wine and unmixed wine suddenly drunk; for the one will produce moisture in the upper belly and wind in the lower, the other throbbing of the veins and heaviness of the head and thirst; and white and dark wine, when people change contrary to habit, even if both are vinous, would nevertheless alter much in the body; so that one would say it is less wonderful that sweet and vinous [wine], suddenly changed, do not have the same power." From Hippocrates the examples written up to this point about the power of habits are enough; Erasistratus, in the second book On Paralysis, wrote roughly as follows: "One who is going to practise medicine properly must make a very thorough examination of habituation and lack of habituation. I mean something like this: those who perform many accustomed labours continue unfatigued, but those who perform a few unaccustomed ones become somewhat fatigued; and some digest accustomed foods that are harder to digest more easily than unaccustomed ones that are easier to digest; and the body seeks out accustomed evacuations, even if they are unprofitable, once they have become habitual, and when deprived of them falls into diseases, as happens with discharges from haemorrhoids and purgings which some make habitual for themselves, and indeed with ulcers that break out from time to time and discharge serum, and as with some who get choleras at certain times. For the body seeks out all such evacuations, though they are unprofitable, and when they do not occur at the accustomed times, those to whom such things are habitual fall into no small affections. Some such things also appear to happen by habituation with the verses and iambics we know: if someone should bid us recite two or three lines from the middle, being unaccustomed to such a thing, we could not readily do so; but coming to these same lines by reciting in order, we will say them readily and easily, and by becoming accustomed we also do the former readily. Something like this also happens: those unaccustomed to learning learn slowly and little, but having become more accustomed they do this much more and more easily. The like occurs with inquiries too: for those wholly unaccustomed to inquiry are blinded and darkened in the first movements of the mind, and at once give up inquiring, wearied in mind and exhausted, no less than those who come to running unaccustomed; but one accustomed to inquiry, penetrating everywhere and searching with his mind and shifting to many places, does not give up the inquiry, resting from the inquiry not merely for part of a day but not even in his whole life; and shifting his mind to other thoughts not foreign to what is sought, he presses on until he comes to the matter in hand. Thus the effects of habituation appear so far to prevail in all our affections alike, both those of the soul and those of the body. Let this be said sufficiently about these matters for the present; but in the general discussions about medicine the things requiring examination are enumerated more fully, if much in medicine is not to go lame." These are the things the most renowned of physicians, Erasistratus and Hippocrates, have said about the power of habits, not attributing their discovery to reasoning but having been taught by what is plainly evident, as indeed [is true] also of other people, as many as do not live like pigs or donkeys but pay attention to the things by which they are helped and harmed. One can hear them every day saying that they are accustomed to this food and this drink and for this reason cannot give them up; for they are also harmed by the changes. They say the same about pursuits too, such as going without baths or bathing, riding or hunting, running or wrestling, wakefulness or sleep, sunning or cooling, cares, and other such things.

Let us, then, disregarding those who think that the aim derived from habits contributes either nothing at all or little to therapy, examine what the cause may be of habit's great power, and whether it is a single one or a different one for each material. By material I mean that in which the habit has been formed, such as, as I said, foods or drinks or exercises or something else of the kind. Let us make our beginning with the things eaten and drunk. Why is it that, of those who habitually eat beef, some are not harmed at all, and some less than before? Or why do some, by nature, right from the start, as Erasistratus himself wrote, digest beef more easily than rock fish? The cause of this has been stated in the examination of the natural faculties, and it will also be stated now a little later in the course of the argument. For now, let us make the beginning of our teaching from those who, through habit, digest any food at all better, taking as a common basis for all these the things that are by nature akin to some people and not akin to others. Now, all these matters have been discussed at greater length in the examination of the natural faculties; but let us begin the argument now too by setting out the concept of digestion. Just as bakers are said to 'cook' bread not when, by grinding and sifting, they break the wheat into fine particles, but when, after doing this, they wet it with water, mix in leaven and knead it, then cover it with something warming and leave it until, as they themselves call it, it has been leavened, and after this bake it in ovens or furnaces, so too with what is swallowed into the stomach we say it has been digested not when it has been broken up and dissolved in it, but when, like the wheat being baked, it has undergone a change in quality. And just as with bread the grain being baked must be brought to a quality akin to us who eat it, so in the belly it must be brought still more to a quality more akin; and I call one quality more akin than another according to its likeness to the body that is to be nourished by it. For different nourishing things are akin to different bodies, and for this reason animals go to the foods akin to them untaught, driven by nature: beasts of burden to grasses, chaff, fodder and barley, lions to flesh, as also leopards and wolves. Just as among animals, then, by genus there is no small difference in the foods akin to each, so too by species within the genera great differences are found: some cannot even taste wine, while others drink a great deal of it without distress; and some, as has been said, eat the flesh of oxen, goats and rams with pleasure and digest it without distress, while others cannot even endure its smell, let alone eating it; and if, for lack of any other food, as happens in famine, they should force themselves to take such meat, they can neither digest it without harm, but their appetite is upset at taking it, and they are at once weighed down, and if a belch comes upon them, they cannot endure even this without distress. That these things evidently are so, one must first remember this: that people take one thing or another more pleasantly according to the affinity of their nature, and go more readily to eating such things, as also to those that have appeared easily digestible to them, but turn away from and flee what is unpleasant and hard to digest, so that habit is a sign of natural affinity. That it also often becomes a cause is clear from those who are at first affected unpleasantly or harmfully by certain things, but who, if they endure habituation to them little by little, are no longer affected either unpleasantly or harmfully. The cause of this too is something like this: just as each of the things eaten and drunk is altered in quality, so it also itself affects in some way that which alters it. One can take clear evidence of this too from the difference in the humours generated by each of the foods: some generate melancholic blood, others phlegmatic blood, or blood containing no little of the bile called pale and yellow, just as some [generate] pure blood. Some difference, then, must necessarily arise in the parts nourished, relative to one another, according to the character of the nourishing blood. And clear evidence of the assimilation of what is nourished to what nourishes is the change of plants and seeds, which often goes so far that what is most harmful in one soil, when transplanted into another soil, becomes not only harmless but even useful. For those who have composed treatises on agriculture and on plants have much experience of these things, as indeed do those who have written on the history of animals, of the change that occurs according to region. Since, then, not only is what nourishes altered by what is nourished, but it also itself in some way alters it with a slight alteration, it is necessary that this slight [alteration] becomes considerable over time, so that the [affinity] from long-standing habits comes to equal natural affinity.

As regards things eaten and drunk, then, I think I have found the cause of the power of habits; let us next look at the things that fall upon us from outside. For these too seem to have a cause the same in kind as those mentioned before. They produce, then, a certain alteration in the body, chiefly of the surface parts, but then also of those in the depth. For the skin is compressed, drawn together, constricted and condensed, first by cooling things, and next the parts continuous with it too; and if the body undergoes the same alteration over a longer time, the deep parts also come to share in the change. But right from the beginning, incidentally, not primarily, change and alteration by the acting cause befall not least the parts lying in the depth: for when the skin is condensed, the heat collects in the depth of the whole body. And just as the cooling cause produces the alterations described, in the same way the heating cause produces those opposite to them. For it is natural for opposites to arise from opposites, some primarily and some incidentally; and it is in these especially that many go wrong, observing certain things brought about incidentally in the same way by opposites, just as, again, opposites often arise from the same causes. Certainly one happens to be deceived in the same way with heating things too. The hot cause, for example the sun, when it is in contact with some body for a long time, produces in it a condition opposite to that at the beginning. For at the beginning, warming us, it diffuses the fluids, relaxes the skin and makes the flesh softer; but if someone spends many days naked in it in summer, his skin becomes parched and hard, and his flesh dry. But in such cases the work is not of the long-continued heat alone but also of the dryness yoked with it. And this often misleads us in our reasonings about causes, when the cause intertwined [with the other] is overlooked. For we ought to bear in mind that moist heat does one thing and dry heat another, which we sometimes fail to do, and for this reason we go wrong, overlooking the proper action of each of the causes; but if one pays attention, he will find each preserved. For just as moisture alone, without evident heat or cold, moistens the body, while heat heats it, so the combination of both evidently does both. This happens in baths of fresh water, while in sun-heating the drying cause is intertwined with the heating one. Such is the summer sun, so that it is likely that those who spend most of their time naked in it, such as reapers and sailors, have their skin become hard and dry, much like that of scaly animals. Just as, then, the natural peculiarities of bodies, the differences of their whole substance, and the differences of the skin in hardness and softness, density and rarity, require different foods and drinks, and are not all affected alike by being heated and cooled, so the [peculiarities] arising through habit, being similar to the natural ones, receive the same benefit and harm as they do from the alteration produced by the cooling and heating things eaten and drunk. For a rare and soft body is easily affected when heated and cooled; but a dense and hard one endures and disregards everything that falls upon it from outside, not only if they heat or cool, but also if something is hard and rough. Hence such [bodies] endure sleeping on the ground, while those in the opposite condition do not bear it: for they are easily bruised and chilled and readily suffer anything whatever.

Such, then, is the account concerning these things; that concerning exercises is as follows. The parts of the body that are exercised become at once stronger and more callused, and for this reason they can bear their proper movements better than other [parts] that are softer and weaker through lack of exercise. This account holds in common also for the exercises of the soul: for we are exercised first with the teachers of letters while still children, and then next with the teachers of rhetoric, of arithmetic and calculation, and of geometry. For since there are faculties in the ruling part of the soul for all the arts, it is necessary that there be one by which we recognise what is consistent and what conflicts, and another by which we remember; we become more intelligent by the first-mentioned, and better at remembering by the second, since all the faculties are by nature such as to be increased and strengthened by exercises, and harmed by idleness, as Plato too somewhere in the Timaeus made plain in this passage, saying in these very words: "Just as we have often said, that three kinds of soul have been housed in us, and each happens to have movements, so in the same way we must now say, as briefly as possible, that the one of them which lives in idleness and keeps its own movements at rest necessarily becomes weakest, and the one that is in exercise strongest; therefore we must take care that they have their movements in due proportion to one another." Having said this first, he says next: "As for the most sovereign kind of soul in us, we must think of it thus: that god has given it to each as a guardian spirit, this which we say dwells at the top of our body and raises us from earth towards our kinship in heaven, since we are a plant not earthly but heavenly, and in saying so we speak most rightly; for from there, whence the first birth of the soul arose, the divine, suspending our head and root, keeps the whole body upright. Now for one who is wholly given over to desires or to rivalries and labours hard at these, all his opinions must necessarily have become mortal, and he must altogether, so far as it is possible to become mortal, fall short of this not even a little, since he has fostered this so much; but for one who has been earnest about love of learning and true wisdom, and has exercised these most of all his [faculties], it is surely wholly necessary that he think immortal and divine thoughts, if indeed he lays hold of truth, and that, so far as human nature can share in immortality, he leave out no part of this; and since he is always tending the divine and keeps well ordered the guardian spirit that dwells with him, he must be happy above others. And the tending of anything by anyone is one: to give to each its own proper nourishment and movements." In these words Plato, speaking of the three kinds of soul, taught us something useful not only for philosophy but also for the health of the body, following Hippocrates in this, who said in general, "use strengthens, idleness wastes", and specifically of exercises again, in saying "let exertions precede food", and of all the particular kinds, "exertions, food, drink, sleep, sex: all in moderation". Therefore here too one must attend closely to what is said; for it admits of a certain mishearing, like all other statements, if one listens carelessly, as some do. For we hold that each of the faculties should be exercised, surely not without the proper limits and measures, with the exercises stretched out so far as to undo the faculty; and likewise that one should use food, drink, sleep and sex in the proper measure, neither falling short nor exceeding. For excesses undo the faculties, while deficiency in each prevents complete benefit by as much as it falls short of due proportion. This too was enjoined by Hippocrates in one case as an example, where he says: "In every movement of the body, when it begins to feel strain, resting at once [keeps it] free of fatigue." And the account, by the kinship of the subjects, has in a way already taught something also about the habits of the soul in memory, reasoning and logical inquiry, which Erasistratus himself also mentioned in his discourse on habits without adding the cause, although not only Hippocrates but also Plato had stated it. For the activity of each of the faculties in its proper and well-proportioned exercises produces vigour in them.

These, then, are the differences of habits according to the power of the materials in which they are formed and of the causes by which they come about. But since Erasistratus said that the body also comes to seek evacuations, when people have become habituated to them, we must examine these too. For we know of some who bleed from the nose, either at certain periods of equal length or irregularly, or who are evacuated through haemorrhoids, or through vomiting, or by diarrhoeas or choleras, and sometimes who voluntarily let blood, either by phlebotomy or by scarifications at the ankles [or through the nose], just as also by purgative drugs, both emetic and laxative; about these too it is useful to consider something. For it does not seem to me that bodies need such evacuations through habit, but that for whatever cause they needed the first evacuation, whether nature brought it about or some person by medical reasoning, so they need the same things again and often for the same reasons. For some, through bad regimens, and some through a bad constitution of the body, accumulating an abundance of blood or a bad state of the humours, are benefited by the evacuations mentioned, when nature or some doctor pours off the excess before the person falls ill. In some who fell ill, the crisis through such excretions was the cure of the disease; and some were treated by doctors who used similar remedies, and then, later caught by a similar disease and treated by the same means, if ever again either a heaviness of the body or some irregularity of the head alone or some other unnatural thing appears in them, they consult the doctors about these, saying they fear being caught by the same diseases by which they were caught before, after similar symptoms had preceded; and then, having escaped the expected disease by anticipating it through some purging or removal of blood, they resort more readily to the same remedy when they perceive some similar symptom befalling them at some later time. And some, even before perceiving [anything], suspecting the appointed time at which in a fixed period they suffered something of this kind, anticipate it by being evacuated, and they call this preventive evacuation a habit that has come about in them, although the body receives no change from such evacuations of the kind it was shown to receive in the cases mentioned before, but suffers the same things from the same cause. If, then, they change their regimen, using less food and adding something to their exercises, they remain free of disease, benefited by the change of habits, not harmed as those mentioned earlier were; for it was not by reason of habit that they happened to be benefited by the evacuations, but because through a bad regimen they were accumulating bad humours and abundance.
